🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

### Source and code identities

- Observed production source: [`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83)

issues.author: bethehand
issues.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A precision on the lm_head finding above: those numbers use the H100 d768–d1536 rungs, because the no-lm_head compute table I started from has no d512 entry. With the Oct 3 refit's exact setting (d512–d1536, one floor shared across both mixes and all 15 progress points), removing only the lm_head FLOPs moves the fitted floor from 1.858 to 1.630 (floors within 10% of the minimum SSE span 1.58–1.68) and the forecast from 2.100 to 2.056. So the compute convention accounts for about 0.044 of the 0.061 gap to the Aug 19 pre-registration, about 72%. d512 is where the convention matters most: counting lm_head multiplies its compute by 2.84, against 2.07 at d768 and 1.33 at d1536. comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld. Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0).

**TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09).** Given one expert E built from the Snowball student B by SFT on GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: plain SFT on E's traces, SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT), and on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts. Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. RS-SFT and OPD are both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering (1.2 / 2.7 pp) is unresolved with one run per arm and two evaluator passes. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K or MATH500. Training cost: plain SFT 61.6 H100-h, RS-SFT 57.4, OPD 376.4 for the full run (286.9 to the selected checkpoint, plus 14–15 per HF export). RS-SFT used ground-truth execution results to select demos; the other arms did not. These numbers measure transfer on seen prompts, not generalization.

**Results (selected checkpoints; CruxEval two-pass means, pass@1 %, 800 problems per direction; "gap closed" = gain over B divided by E's gain over B).**

| Model | CruxEval input | CruxEval output | Gap closed (in / out) | GSM8K | MATH500 | Training H100-h |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B (student) | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 | — |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — |
| E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 |
| Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 | 61.6 |
| RS-SFT on execution-correct E demos, 283 of 376 updates | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 | 57.4 (full run) |
| OPD from E, 75 of 100 updates | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 | 286.9 to the checkpoint; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export |

**Models.** Student B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`. E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`. E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B.

**Benchmark.** CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop.

**Frozen evaluator.** Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy `c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2`, vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes.

**Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms).
- Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100).
- RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100).
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron).
- Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction.

**Artifacts.** Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: marin-community/skyrl run p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`, RS-SFT `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`, OPD `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`. Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/<record>/record.json`.

**Not in scope.** Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval).

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher.
- 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used.
- 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain.
- 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm.
- 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris.
- 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

🤖
# Research

Teacher training and three transfer arms make this a gated experiment. As of 23:29 UTC, the owner has submitted the W&B-corrected teacher retry; startup, optimizer progress, and export remain unconfirmed ([latest status](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6048938002)). No open PR targets #9920, while the owner is already preparing the recipe on `task/133`; the earlier coding-teacher spike [#9528](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9528) ended without a usable MOPD transfer result.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT specification and training setup
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned SkyRL experiment and export contract
- [`experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path

# Proposed Fix

1. Follow the submitted teacher retry through a completed update, full training, and verified HF exports. Evaluate the planned exports with the frozen CruxEval/GSM8K configuration. Stop the transfer arms unless E clears the stated +10-point gate on both CruxEval directions without a GSM8K drop beyond noise.
2. Pin E, B, prompt IDs, tokenizer/template, grader, evaluator, and one eight-sample-per-prompt teacher generation artifact. Build unfiltered SFT from samples 1–4 and rejection-sampled SFT from up to four execution-correct samples. Record missing-correct-sample prompts, actual supervised tokens, and teacher-generation GPU-hours; a matched prompt set alone does not equalize training tokens.
3. Start OPD from the same B and prompts. Check teacher/student token-score alignment and one update plus export before the full run. Match the planned sweep and student update budget across arms, and record teacher-scoring GPU-hours separately.
4. Evaluate every selected arm twice with the same pinned evaluator on CruxEval input, CruxEval output, and GSM8K. Report each arm's accuracy, `(arm − B) / (E − B)` per direction, run-to-run spread, prompts and tokens consumed, and total GPU-hours. Label gains as transfer on the trained test prompts; this protocol cannot establish held-out generalization.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`.
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 GLM 5.3 CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy c131e5ab, vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model (correct / n): B 1/26, 1/71 (record c731); E 2/26, 1/71 (pass 1, record 8a4b; the slice was selected by E failing 8 samples, so E's low score here is selection-induced); plain SFT final 0/26, 3/71 (pass 1, record 6676); OPD update 50 0/26, 2/71 (record 8529). Selected checkpoints (pass 1 / pass 2): RS 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71 (covered 647/774, 609/729 and 638/774, 620/729); OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71; plain 400 pass 2 0/26, 4/71; E pass 2 1/26, 4/71. Under this protocol it is a difficult slice; this does not establish that it is unsolvable or that missing demos cannot hurt RS. Headline scores keep the full 1,600 denominator. Script: `experiments/tutorials/slice_cruxeval.py` (joins eval rows to CruxEval ids via the captured prompt text).

## Costs (H100-hours)

Rules: per-checkpoint costs come from allocation-to-checkpoint timestamps, not pro-rating a run total (startup/export overheads differ); teacher-demo generation is reported as shared physical cost and logical per-arm share; one prompt epoch is not matched tokens (OPD 4 samples/prompt vs SFT 1).

- E: 35.9 successful + 15.3 aborted attempts; E+ 29.9.
- GLM traces: relay (no GPU-hours on our side); E demos k=8: task `/karan/task145-e-demos-k8-20261008/inference-e07ff…/0`, 8 × H100, one attempt, 1h49m39.84s = 14.622 for all 12,800 demos, counted once across SFT+RS (a 1/8 plain share is an allocation convention, not a measured cost); pilot child 5m25.9s = 0.724. Serve children show killed/Terminated at normal collector teardown; completed parents and complete.json establish success (job counter preemptions=1 but only attempt 0 exists; not a failed collection).
- Plain SFT: 61.6 (4 GPU tasks × 8 × 1h55m26s; in-gang startup/training/saves/exports).
- RS-SFT: 57.4 (4 GPU tasks × 8 × 1h47m35s; same accounting; demo grading on CPU in an isolated container, not counted).
- OPD: smoke/debug/export 73.5 (attempt 1 27.1, attempt 2 27.2, export 19.2); full-run startup failure 4.6; full run 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m30s); exports 14.4 + 15.1 + 14.2 + 15.1 = 58.8. Total OPD arm (excluding evals): 513.3; full run + exports only: 435.2. Allocation-to-checkpoint (48 GPUs from task start 20:32:45 UTC 2026-10-08 to the checkpoint's export-request log line; includes the ~24 min startup before step 1 at 20:57): update 25 at 23:01:18 → 2h28m33s = 118.8; update 50 at 00:40:01 → 4h07m16s = 197.8; update 75 at 02:31:21 → 5h58m36s = 286.9; update 100 at 04:22:19 → 7h49m34s = 375.7 (job total 376.4 incl. teardown). Epoch wall times: 2h28m (incl. startup), 1h39m, 1h51m, 1h51m. Each checkpoint also needs one ~14–15 H100-h export job before evaluation.
- Evals: ~25 min × 8 per CruxEval pass ≈ 3.3 each. Evaluation overhead from infra failures: RS step-94 group …015842 (serve unreachable, GPU time not retrieved, cancelled) and RS step-375 group …030945 (serve preempted 6×, eval client held the stale endpoint; serve task 1h02m ≈ 8.3 H100-h, cancelled) and OPD step-75 group …033025 (two preempted serve attempts ≈ 0.8 H100-h).

## Material failures / tweaks

- Levanter HF export from an S3 reference checkpoint (fixed: `hf_save_reference_code=False` plumbing).
- MarinSkyRL: teachers only from HF repo ids (added S3 staging); export document kept the distillation
  objective without teachers (fixed); learner-node host OOM at checkpoint save at 512 GB (reserved 1024 GB).
- Evalchemy chat client sends no temperature/seed (all runs at vLLM default 1.0); GPQA-D needs HF token and
  a smaller generation cap (reference only).
- Eval runner keeps a stale serve address after the serve job is preempted and re-registers elsewhere (two RS eval groups lost this way; relaunched as fresh groups). Not fixed; worth an issue.

## Caveats

Test-exposed prompts (all arms train on the eval set); RS-SFT uses ground-truth execution correctness to filter demos (verifier access that plain SFT and reward-replace OPD do not have) plus 8 teacher samples per prompt; supervised-token budgets differ across arms; gains include response-shape change (B leaves no
final content in 1,110/1,600 CruxEval responses; E ~90); single-pass noise; SFT and OPD differ in
batch/update geometry (16 rows/update vs 64 prompts × 4 rollouts), optimizer implementation (Levanter vs
Megatron AdamW) and data (fixed demos vs fresh rollouts).

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Task generation needs to grade a final state that was not produced by model inference: a workspace or reply assembled by a builder program (to check a grader against known-good and known-bad candidates before any rollout), and a candidate an adversary assembled on its own machine (to let a red-teamer call the real verifier as a tool). Both need the same preparation a rollout gets: the task machine with resources and setup commands, supplied files and commands applied on top, the lowered verifier machine when the grader has an environment, and the grader's own collect and artifact steps.

`taskcompendium.runtime.grading.grade_in_sandbox` and `task_grading.sandbox_grade` grade a supplied `GradingAttempt`, but they do not prepare a task machine, so they cannot serve a `ScriptGrader` with `collect` or `artifacts`, supplied commands, or a candidate that lives in machine state rather than in the conversation.

Proposed: `ShellboxRolloutEngine.grade_state(lowered: LoweredTaskSpec, state: SuppliedState) -> GradeResult`, where `SuppliedState(messages, resources: tuple[TaskResource, ...] = (), commands: tuple[str, ...] = ())` installs the resources under `/` after the task machine is prepared, runs the commands as setup commands run, then grades through the same path as a rollout (verifier machine created from the lowered runtime). A failed supplied resource or command is reported as a new `RolloutOperation.STATE`. A ShellSim task rejects supplied resources carrying `mtime_ns` before any machine starts, matching lowering's rule for task resources.

This is what PR #9838 implements; the issue tracks the need so the PR can be judged against it after the #9798 contract change (the PR is being re-expressed onto `main` at or after 4b454d0278).

comments.body: PTB is '1989 Wall Street Journal (WSJ) articles'. We want our model to understand what happened in the 1980s in general.. so having the facts of this eval in the training data is intentional. Will see what comes up from scanning our data in this 6k step range.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Data scan result: PTB's own text was in the training stream ~500 steps before the 210k checkpoint (hypothesis 2, contamination).**

**Method.** I rebuilt the hero's exact training stream from the run's logged data config: launch commit `ad754c6d67`, seed 0, the 0 / 108,000 / 312,192 mix stages, and the block shuffle. Then I read every sequence trained in steps **204,000–216,000**: 12,000 steps × 11,264 sequences × 4,096 tokens, about 554B tokens over 48 CPU jobs on cw-us-east-02a. The scan searched for PTB-specific lowercase phrases, their normal-cased counterparts, and runs of ` <unk>`.

**Result.** A block of about **231 sequences (~1M tokens)** in source **`c13q3`** at **steps 209,272–209,669** contains Penn Treebank text expanded into sliding n-gram windows (`<s> <s> … <word>` per line). It reads like an NLP exercise repository: it also has NMT training notes and scraped request headers. It includes the exact sentences in our PTB eval, e.g. `los angeles financier marvin`, `in london british airways chairman lord king`, `the stock of ual corp. continued`, `the dow industrials were off N points`. A related source, `c28q1`, has n-gram log-probability tables over the same text around step 206.3k (`lg P(corp. | acquire ual)`).

| Lowercase PTB-format hits | steps 204k–210k | steps 210k–216k |
|---|---|---|
| `los angeles financier` | 3 | 0 |
| `british airways chairman` | 3 | 0 |
| `ual corp` | 26 | 0 |

Normal-cased news about the same entities appears about equally in both ranges:

| Normal-cased hits | steps 204k–210k | steps 210k–216k |
|---|---|---|
| `Marvin Davis` | 331 | 332 |
| `UAL Corp` | 226 | 230 |
| `British Airways chairman` | 25 | 27 |

So general knowledge of the 1989 story is steady. What changed before 210k is exposure to the PTB text itself, which the checkpoint partly retained and which had faded by 216k. "Lord King" alone produced thousands of false positives ("Sovereign Lord King James…"), so those hits are excluded.

**300-character chunks: PTB eval text vs. the training document**

PTB (Paloma `ptb` val):
```
this is a total <unk> for takeover-stock traders one investment banker said 
 los angeles financier marvin davis who put united in play with a $ N billion bid two months ago last night <unk> both a ray of hope and an extra element of uncertainty by saying he remains interested in acquiring ual 
 but
```
Training stream (`c13q3`, step 209,550):
```
 traders one investment
for takeover-stock traders one investment banker
takeover-stock traders one investment banker said
<s> <s> <s> <s> <s> los
<s> <s> <s> <s> los angeles
<s> <s> <s> los angeles financier
<s> <s> los angeles financier marvin
<s> los angeles financier <NAME>
los angeles financier
```

PTB:
```
in london british airways chairman lord king was quoted in the times as declaring he is not prepared to take my shareholders into a <unk> deal 
 observers said it appeared that british air was angered at the way the bid has <unk> into confusion as well as by the banks ' effort to round up financing 
```
Training stream (`c13q3`, step 209,665):
```
<s> <s> <s> <s> in london
<s> <s> <s> in london british
<s> <s> in london british airways
<s> in london british airways chairman
in london british airways chairman lord
london british airways chairman lord king
british airways chairman lord king was
airways chairman lord king was quoted
chairman lor
```

The training copy has "marvin davis" replaced with `<NAME>` in most windows, presumably by PII scrubbing. One window, `los angeles financier marvin`, kept the first name because the scrubber only caught "marvin davis" as a pair. That is the token the 210k checkpoint predicted at 0.80. It also explains why every checkpoint already completes `marvin → davis`: that part is general knowledge, not this document.

**Takeaways**
- The 210k drop in PTB loss (about −0.2 nats, spread across almost every line) comes from verbatim exposure to the eval text in an n-gram layout roughly 330–730 steps earlier. It is not a capability change. 210k still misses PTB's genuinely surprising words ("declaring", "my"), which fits brief, partial exposure.
- Paloma PTB is contaminated in the hero mix, at least in `c13q3` and `c28q1`. Its curve will spike whenever those windows come up in the data order, so it shouldn't be read as a quality signal. Wikitext-103 and the other public eval sets may warrant the same scan.

Raw hits: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/larry/scratch/hero_scan/full/*.jsonl`. Scanner: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/scan_training_data.py` on local branch `hero-data-scan`, not pushed.

comments.body:
🤖 **The contaminated document, and every step that reads it**

**What it is.** One GitHub repository dump in source `c13q3`, **`quanpn90/torch-nplm`**: a Torch implementation of Bengio et al. (2003), with the name scrubbed to `<NAME>` in the README. It is **1,385,899 tokens** (4.83M characters), a single BOS…EOS document that spans 340 training sequences of 4,096 tokens.

| File | Characters |
|---|---|
| README.md | 260 |
| extract_ngrams.py | 2,308 |
| train.lua | 12,261 |
| **data/ptb/test.6grams** | **2,543,118** |
| **data/ptb/valid.6grams** | **2,262,165** |
| util/BatchLoader.lua | 4,901 |
| util/IdentityLinear.lua | 985 |

About 99.6% of the document is the **full PTB test and validation sets as sliding 6-gram windows**. `valid.6grams` starts `<s> <s> <s> <s> <s> consumers / … / consumers may want to move their / may want to move their telephones …`, which is exactly the start of Paloma's `ptb` eval document. So the whole Paloma PTB eval set is in the training data, with each word appearing in 6 overlapping windows.

First 500 characters:
```
Repository: quanpn90/torch-nplm

File: README.md

Neural probabilistic language model (<NAME>, 2003) implemented in Torch.

GPU supported for fast training.

Hierarchical supported for fast softmax-ing on a large vocabulary. 

HSM borrowed from https://github.com/yoonkim/lstm-char-cnn


File: extract_ngrams.py
#!/usr/bin/python
import sys

# This script extracts n-grams from a set of PREPROCESSED text files (train, set, valid)

data_dir = sys.argv[1]
ngram_order = int(sys.argv[2])

tra
```

**Every step that reads it over the full 390,251-step schedule.** I inverted the mixture and block shuffle using the run's logged data config: launch commit `ad754c6d67`, seed 0, the 0 / 108,000 / 312,192 stages, and `c13q3` at 69.8M sequences per epoch. The document straddles two 256-sequence shuffle blocks, which land in different shuffle windows, so each epoch reads it in two bursts:

| Epoch | Document part | Sequences | Steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | code + first ~60% of `test.6grams` | 112 | **176,080–176,355** |
| 0 | rest of `test.6grams` + **all of `valid.6grams` (Paloma PTB)** | 228 | **209,390–209,669** |
| 1 | code + first ~60% of `test.6grams` | 112 | 327,205–327,493 *(future)* |
| 1 | rest of `test.6grams` + **all of `valid.6grams`** | 228 | **362,280–362,578** *(future)* |

**Implications**
- The 210k checkpoint was saved about 330–610 steps after the hero trained on the entire Paloma PTB eval set. That explains the drop, and its fading by 216k.
- **The PTB eval should drop again right after step ~362.3k**, when epoch 1 reaches the same block; that's in the cooldown stage. It's a useful sanity check that this explanation is right. The ~176k and ~327k bursts carry only PTB test-split text, not the Paloma eval text.
- Other copies of PTB in the mix, for example the n-gram probability tables in `c28q1` around step 206.3k, aren't covered by this mapping. A dedup or decontamination pass against Paloma would find them.

Files: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/larry/scratch/hero_scan/docs/` holds the full document text (`doc_209550_4116.txt`), `summary.json`, and `torch_nplm_steps.json`, which maps every read to its step and row. comments.body: @ClassicLarry, I went through the public W&B evals: all 16 Paloma and 7 Uncheatable subsets, every eval from step 2,999 to 227,999. I also ran the decon matcher on the torch-nplm files. Here are four results that may help the scan. **1. PTB has drops the torch-nplm reads don't explain** | Evals | PTB loss | Note | |---|---|---| | 101,999 → **104,999** → 107,999 | 2.143 → **1.961** → 2.109 | A one-eval drop with no mapped read nearby | | 188,999 → **191,999** | 2.115 → **2.015** | Drops 0.10 and stays below 2.08 through 227,999 | | 173,999 → **176,999** → 179,999 | 2.141 → **2.099** → 2.114 | Just after the 176,080–176,355 read, which has only the PTB *test* split | | 203,999 → **206,999** → 209,999 | 2.079 → **1.903** → 1.712 | The first half comes before the 209,390 read; it fits the `c28q1` tables at ~206.3k | The 176,999 row is a natural control. That read had PTB test text but none of the eval sentences. It moved the eval 0.029 below the average of its two neighbours, while the curve otherwise stays between 2.113 and 2.141 from 155,999 to 188,999. By the same measure, 104,999 is 0.165 below its neighbours, close to 209,999's 0.187. So I'd guess another copy of the validation text was read in steps **102,000–104,999**. If your scanner can run on that range, and on **189,000–191,999**, that would test it. **2. WikiText-103 shows the same pattern; general Wikipedia doesn't** At steps 125,999 / 128,999 / 131,999 / 134,999, `wikitext_103` reads 1.707 / **1.558** / 1.638 / 1.684. Over the same evals, `m2d2_wikipedia_unsplit` reads 1.828 / 1.827 / 1.823 / 1.824. Smaller one-sided drops recur at 137,999, 152,999, 203,999 and 212,999–215,999. None of them shows up in m2d2_wikipedia. A 0.15 drop on the WikiText eval with flat general Wikipedia looks like a document containing the eval text itself, not a Wikipedia-heavy stretch. Candidate windows: - **126,000–128,999**; - **210,000–212,999**, which your 204k–216k scan already covers. Re-running it with a few WikiText eval sentences may be the cheapest first check. **3. Decon would have missed torch-nplm even with Paloma indexed** Paloma isn't in the decon eval corpus, and `wikitext` is excluded on purpose (`DECON_EXCLUDED_EVAL_TASKS`, #6852 cluster A). I indexed the PTB validation text (Paloma's `ptb`) anyway to test the matcher. I ran the matching functions in `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/decon.py` unchanged, using the `reference_pipeline.py` settings: 13-grams, overlap ≥ 0.5, ≥ 2 matched features, paragraphs split on `\n\n`. When most lines of a paragraph are windows that shift by one token, stitch them back into running text, drop ``, and score the result as an extra paragraph. Overlap goes back to 1.000. In 5,724 ordinary code and text files (the Marin repo and the CPython 3.12 standard library), the pass triggered on none of 241,449 paragraphs. Details are on #6852, the issue about this matcher's recall. So one store-wide pass may be cheaper than scanning step ranges. Run decon in flag-only mode against Paloma `ptb` and `wikitext_103`, with the stitching pass, and then run `find_doc_steps.py` on what it flags. Raw copies would score about 1.0. **4. issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Running `uv run pytest lib/taskcompendium/tests experiments/post_training/task_curation/tests` in one invocation fails about 40 runtime tests, while each directory passes alone. Something in one tree leaks process state (fixtures, environment, module caches) into the other. Find the shared state and isolate it so a combined run passes.

Part of #9798.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The combined command uses the root pytest config, which leaves `pytest-asyncio` in strict mode; TaskCompendium's package config uses auto mode. Its 18 unmarked async test functions fail before execution (the first after 94 passes). Zephyr also chooses a regional GCS bucket for temporary shards in pipeline tests; one test timed out after 60 seconds and passed in 3.5 seconds with a local `MARIN_PREFIX`.

**Relevant code**
- [`pyproject.toml#L523-L550`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/pyproject.toml#L523-L550) - root pytest settings
- [`lib/taskcompendium/pyproject.toml#L24-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/taskcompendium/pyproject.toml#L24-L25) - package async mode
- [`test_convert_executable.py#L236`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/taskcompendium/tests/test_convert_executable.py#L236) - first failing async test
- [`zephyr/context.py#L276-L277`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a95cc117e21c03400b27febfb9e64d7176d744e9/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/context.py#L276-L277) - remote temporary storage default

# Proposed Fix

Mark TaskCompendium's async tests explicitly and give its tests a per-test local `MARIN_PREFIX`. These changes keep the root pytest mode unchanged and keep test shards off GCS. With equivalent command-line settings, the combined suite passed 889 tests and skipped 9 in 46.81 seconds on `a95cc117e2`; I will send a focused PR against #9798's branch.

issues.author: asartran
issues.body:
The `github.ci` arm of `scripts/ci/wait_for.py` never fires when the installed `gh` lacks `gh pr checks --json`. It reports `0 checks, none failing, not all done` until the overall timeout, even after every check has finished or one has failed. Two PR monitors in the #9812 work lost their CI signal this way: one waited the full 12 hours, the other sat idle for 2h40m.

Reproduce:
1. Use `gh` 2.45.0 (the Ubuntu 24.04 package): `gh pr checks 9860 --repo marin-community/marin --json name,bucket,state` prints `unknown flag: --json` to stderr and nothing to stdout.
2. Run `uv run scripts/ci/wait_for.py --timeout 1h "github.ci 9860"` on a PR whose checks have all finished.

Expected: the arm fires with the CI result, or the command fails with an error saying `gh` is too old.

Cause: `gh_pr_checks` (`scripts/ci/wait_for.py:171`) treats empty stdout as "no checks registered yet" and ignores the exit status and stderr, so the `--json` error looks like a PR with no checks and `evaluate_ci` keeps waiting.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`github.ci` calls `gh_pr_checks()`, which treats empty stdout as an unregistered check set without inspecting the command exit code. An older `gh` exits nonzero for unsupported `--json`, so the selector repeatedly reports zero checks until timeout.

**Relevant code**
- [`wait_for.py#L170-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/wait_for.py#L170-L189) — reads check output
- [`wait_for.py#L534-L557`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/wait_for.py#L534-L557) — evaluates CI state

# Proposed Fix

`CiSource.check()` passes rows from `gh_pr_checks()` to `evaluate_ci()`; the failed `gh` command currently supplies an empty list. Raise `GhError` when stdout is empty and the exit code is nonzero, retaining empty rows for a successful command with no registered checks. Add a regression using a fake older `gh` executable.

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
`shellbox.Machine` has no operation that stops processes a command left behind. Each Docker exec runs under `sh -c` in its own `setsid` session, and the backend only interrupts the command's process group on timeout or cancellation, so a background loop started by an agent command outlives that command and keeps running on the machine.

This matters when a task grades on the agent machine. In #9769 the verifier writes `verdict.json` to a fresh `mktemp -d` directory and the engine reads it in the same exec, but a surviving agent process running as the same user can still scan for the new directory and rewrite the verdict while the verifier runs. `FileReward` has the same exposure at its fixed reward paths. The engine cannot sweep processes itself: on Docker the container's init and any daemons started by setup look the same as the agent's orphans from inside the container.

Reproduce:
1. Run a shell task whose agent executes `while :; do printf '{"status":"scored","reward":1}' > /logs/verifier/verdict.json; done &` and then finishes.
2. Grade with a verdict-file verifier on the agent machine.
3. The loop is still running after the agent command returns and can overwrite the verifier's output.

Expected: before grading, the engine can ask the machine to terminate every process started by agent commands, leaving the container init and processes started by setup or by the grader untouched.

Done when:
- `Machine` exposes an operation that terminates the processes started by a given set of commands (or by all agent commands since a marker), on the Docker, Iris and ShellSim backends.
- The rolloutengine verdict-file and file-reward graders call it before running a verifier on the agent machine.
- A test shows a background writer started by an agent command cannot replace the verdict.

Context: the Codex P1 thread on #9769, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9769#discussion_r4201632563 (thread PRRT_kwDOLj5faM6ps_0m).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`_ShellboxTaskSession.advance()` runs agent `sh -c` commands on the task machine, and `_grade_rollout()` later runs collection and the verifier there when no separate verifier environment is configured; `Machine` has no way to identify or stop processes left by the agent. PR #9769's fresh verdict directory narrows the race, but a live agent process can discover it while grading. No open PR found in the duplicate-work check implements this cleanup; #9769 is still open, and #9844 changes Iris exec retry behavior in an overlapping file.

**Relevant code**

- [`machine.py#L138-L153`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9859a4e80c57e8a6290220fafc6896a470c6e62/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/machine.py#L138-L153) — shared machine contract
- [`docker/machine.py#L52-L83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9859a4e80c57e8a6290220fafc6896a470c6e62/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/docker/machine.py#L52-L83) — exec lifetime
- [`iris/machine.py#L151-L189`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e9859a4e80c57e8a6290220fafc6896a470c6e62/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py#L151-L189) — remote exec lifetime
- [`task_session.py#L143-L175`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7e2196900094fddcaf9c3ce2f9c7f49e3e4f72ad/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/task_session.py#L143-L175) — agent command and grade boundary
- [`grading.py#L95-L128`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7e2196900094fddcaf9c3ce2f9c7f49e3e4f72ad/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py#L95-L128) — same-machine verifier path

# Proposed Fix

## Design

Add an opaque, machine-owned process scope to Shellbox: `open_process_scope() -> ProcessScope`, `run(command, *, scope: ProcessScope | None = None) -> Result`, and `terminate_process_scope(scope) -> None`. Run only agent shell calls in the scope. Setup, health checks, artifact transfer, and verifier commands remain outside it. Termination must be idempotent, prevent new commands in that scope, wait until its live processes are gone, and raise if the backend cannot establish that result. Update every `Machine` implementation to satisfy the contract or report unsupported scope creation explicitly; Docker/gVisor, Iris, and ShellSim are required for this issue.

First test a worker-owned, per-scope process container (a cgroup v2 scope is one candidate) on Docker and Iris gVisor. It must retain detached descendants, including children that call `setsid` or double-fork, while preserving container init and setup daemons. A `killpg` or parent-PID scan does not meet that contract. If either backend cannot provide this containment, reject same-machine scoped grading there and use a separate verifier environment. For ShellSim, terminate retained simulated jobs; if its synchronous runner cannot retain any, prove that invariant with a behavior test and make termination explicit. The Docker/gVisor implementation can share the Docker path; QEMU and Daytona must either implement the scope or reject tasks that require it before agent execution.

Create one scope after task setup, attach it to each agent shell command, and terminate it before `verifier.collect`, private file installation, or verifier execution. For staged tasks, terminate the stage's scope before its grade and open a new scope for the next stage. A failed termination must prevent the verifier from running and surface as an infrastructure failure, never a reward. Keep a separate verifier machine for adversarial file and verdict grading: stopping processes cannot undo agent changes to setup daemons or private paths made before the stop.

## Costs and risks

The change crosses the Shellbox contract and every backend, and PR #9769's Rollout Engine code is still on a stacked branch. Backend containment is the feasibility gate; silently treating process-group termination as complete would leave the reported race open.

## Testing

Start with a failing Rollout Engine regression: an agent command leaves a bounded writer running, the verifier writes a lower reward, and the observed grade must be the verifier's result. Add backend behavior tests that detach a child, terminate the scope, and verify the child stops while a setup daemon survives; also cover repeated termination and failure before grading. Use the existing local Iris RPC fixture and ShellSim suite, with a Docker-marked test for the real container boundary and an Iris sandbox check in dedicated CI. Test FileReward, VerdictReward, and a stage boundary. Run `uv run pytest lib/shellbox/tests/ lib/rolloutengine/tests/`, `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files --fix`, and the pre-PR review when implementing.

## Open questions

- Which worker-side containment primitive is available for scoped execs on Iris gVisor and Docker? Confirm this with a detached-child proof before selecting the implementation.
- Should same-machine file/verdict grading be accepted for untrusted root agents after cleanup? I recommend requiring a separate verifier environment for that threat model, even when scope termination succeeds.

comments.body:
🤖 The reported verdict overwrite path is no longer present on `main`. [#9937](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9937) requires separate Harbor verifier mode, and RolloutEngine's `grade_in_sandbox` creates a fresh machine for verdict-file and `FileReward` grading. [#9769](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9769) closed without merging. Agent processes can still race output capture and `ScriptGrader.collect` on the task machine, so stable collection remains an open problem.

I checked the current Docker boundary: a command cannot create a nested PID namespace (`unshare -Urpf` returns `EPERM`) or a cgroup (`/sys/fs/cgroup` is mounted read-only). Killing the recorded process group would stop the reported background loop, but a child that calls `setsid` survives. Iris currently exposes exec through its worker RPC, without a worker-owned process scope or snapshot operation. A `Machine` method backed by process-group signals would not meet this issue's “every process” contract.

I have not opened a PR for that incomplete cleanup. I recommend narrowing this issue to stable artifact collection and defining a worker-owned freeze/snapshot boundary for Docker and Iris, with a test that covers a detached child and confirms setup daemons survive. The existing fresh verifier machine already protects the verdict and reward paths.

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Since #9967, `rolloutengine.machines` and `rolloutengine.lowering` import `shellbox.backends.local.machine` at module import time, which imports `bubblewrap_bin`, a Linux-only dependency. Importing `rolloutengine` on macOS therefore fails, and every project that imports it for lowering or validation (Taskforge does both) can no longer run its unit tests or type checks on a developer laptop; the only way is a Linux container.

Only the lock-only grader path needs the local backend. Proposed: import the local backend lazily inside the lock-only branch of `_acquire_machine` and `validate_lowered_task`, or guard the module import so that `LocalMachineFactory` is unavailable (and lock-only graders rejected with a clear error) on platforms without bubblewrap, instead of failing the whole package import.

Related: the lock-only path selects itself with `isinstance(factory, LocalMachineFactory)` (`lowering.py` and `_acquire_machine`), so a wrapping factory (a timing or host-checking wrapper that delegates to a `LocalMachineFactory` and reports `backend == Backend.LOCAL`) cannot serve lock-only graders. Dispatching on `factory.backend` would let wrappers through, which the `MachineFactory` protocol's `backend` property seems meant for.

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`rolloutengine.lowering` and `rolloutengine.machines` import the local backend during module loading; `machines` also reaches it through `taskcompendium.runtime.local`. That backend imports Linux-only `bubblewrap_bin`, so macOS cannot import RolloutEngine. Lock-only validation rejects wrappers using `isinstance`, and machine acquisition repeats that check. No open PR addresses this regression.

**Relevant code**
- [`lowering.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/lowering.py#L8) — eager import and concrete-type validation.
- [`machines.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/machines.py#L108) — acquisition rejects wrapped factories.
- [`runtime/local.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/local.py#L25) — another eager local-backend import.
- [`machine.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/local/machine.py#L26) — imports `bubblewrap_bin`.

# Proposed Fix

`lower_task()` calls validation, which rejects a wrapped local factory before rollout; `_acquire_machine()` would reject it again. Use the factory's `backend` for validation and acquisition, carry the lock runtime mount in the `HostImage` request so wrappers can delegate it, and defer local-backend imports until local grading is selected. Add regression coverage for wrapped grading and import without `bubblewrap_bin`.
