issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Sandbox pods created by shellbox's Iris backend cannot pull images from the task registry `envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app`, on CoreWeave as well as on GCP.

Observed on `cw-rno2a` with a gVisor sandbox for `envreg.208261-marin-gpu.coreweave.app/capability-infra/taskforge-grader-base@sha256:63eb0b5c3efb5b2e3def1e81f9e076a4c62a077ad5f631cfef95ea9f441240b3` (a public-content image published by `skopeo copy` with the `capability-registry-publisher` credential): `ImagePullBackOff`, then the 600 s sandbox timeout, then the grader timed out. The same sandbox with `python:3.12-slim` was ready in 20 s and graded. Earlier probes on the GCP workers failed the same way ("workers cannot pull from envreg", recorded on the Taskforge side since 2026-10-05).

Task generation and curation publish every task image and the grader image to envreg by digest, so every image-backed task and every script-graded task is unrunnable on Iris until sandbox pods carry a pull credential for that registry, or the images are mirrored to a registry the clusters already pull from.

Asks: (1) a cluster-wide image pull secret for envreg on the sandbox pod spec (all Iris clusters, both providers), or guidance on which registry Taskforge should publish to instead; (2) the registry speaks only Basic auth (`WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="envgen"`), so if a scoped read-only credential is preferred it has to be created on the registry side.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Shellbox passes the digest-pinned image to Iris as `task_image`. CoreWeave task pods have no `imagePullSecrets` field, while GCP workers pull through Docker on the host; a Kubernetes pull secret would fix only the first path. Taskforge's envreg credential reaches its separate push job, not the sandbox pull. The earlier [registry issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7719) records a preference for public task images, and open [#9784](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9784) owns the Taskforge publisher, so this should be resolved there rather than in a parallel PR.

**Relevant code**
- [`machine.py#L304-L320`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048d657b76eab81e208f31af9ebd33db4/lib/shellbox/src/shellbox/backends/iris/machine.py#L304-L320) — sandbox image submission.
- [`tasks.py#L1062-L1093`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048d657b76eab81e208f31af9ebd33db4/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L1062-L1093) — Kubernetes pod spec.
- [`docker.py#L950-L978`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048d657b76eab81e208f31af9ebd33db4/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/docker.py#L950-L978) — GCP worker pull.
- [`build_image_job.py#L264-L290`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a158af81ebc9c32a134de828c332af2088f4c85a/lib/taskforge/scripts/build_image_job.py#L264-L290) — publisher and digest readback.
- [`image-push.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048d657b76eab81e208f31af9ebd33db4/lib/iris/docs/image-push.md) — GHCR and GCP mirror route.

# Proposed Fix: public Taskforge image package

## Design

Publish public-content task images and the grader base into one `ghcr.io/marin-community/taskforge-images` package. Make that package public before switching consumers: [GHCR supports anonymous pulls of public images](https://docs.github.com/en/packages/working-with-a-github-packages-registry/working-with-the-container-registry), while Iris already pulls GHCR directly on CoreWeave and through Artifact Registry mirrors on GCP. Keep the existing separate build and push jobs and digest-pinned references. In #9784, point the push job at this package, supply a publisher credential with package write access, adapt manifest readback to GHCR authentication, and republish the grader base with its new digest. Update dependent Taskforge references after #9784 lands.

## Costs / risks

GHCR package visibility is a package-level decision; the images and their contents will be public. The publisher credential still needs protection in the push job. A private-image design instead needs a registry-side read-only credential plus *both* Kubernetes pod pull configuration and GCP worker Docker authentication; adding only `imagePullSecrets` leaves GCP broken.

## Testing and rollout

Before changing Taskforge's image references, confirm the new digest resolves with a fresh, empty `DOCKER_CONFIG`, then run the same digest through Shellbox on `cw-rno2a` and a GCP Iris worker. Run one script-graded task to exercise the grader base; check task events for image pull failures and confirm the sandbox receives no registry credential. Keep the old envreg references until both providers pass.

## Open question

Are all generated task images approved for public distribution? If any contain private material, retain those on a separate private-image path and design cross-provider read authentication before running them on Iris.

issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Iris caches a job's environment before the job's own code runs, so a job that scrubs secrets from `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` at startup still hands the unscrubbed environment to any non-sandbox child job it launches.

Observed on `cw-us-east-02a` during a Zephyr feasibility spike for Taskforge: the Taskforge queue job removes `GLM_API_TOKEN`, `WANDB_API_KEY` and the other host secrets from its environment at start (`scrub_child_environment`), and afterwards both `os.environ` and `IRIS_JOB_ENV` are clean. The job environment Iris had already cached still held `GLM_API_TOKEN` and `WANDB_API_KEY`, so a non-sandbox child job would inherit them. Sandbox children (ShellSim, bwrap, gVisor) received no env in this run; gVisor sandboxes did see the `IRIS_*` variables and the Kubernetes service addresses, including the controller's.

Asks: (1) a documented way for a job to launch children with an explicit environment that does not include the parent's cached env (an allowlist on the child job spec, or a per-submission `inherit_env=False`); (2) sandbox pods should not receive `IRIS_*` variables or the controller's service address unless the submitter asks for them, since model-controlled code runs there.

Related earlier notes on the Taskforge side: CoreWeave `task_env` injecting object-store keys into pods (not reproduced on `cw-rno2a` in this spike) and child jobs inheriting a parent's explicit `-e` secrets.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`build_common_iris_env()` snapshots a job's submitted variables into `IRIS_JOB_ENV`; `get_job_info()` reads that snapshot, and `IrisClient.submit()` merges it into every non-sandbox child. Scrubbing `os.environ` after startup leaves the snapshot intact. #9817 already isolates `CONTAINER_PROFILE_SANDBOX` jobs, including their environment and controller address; the remaining gap is a clean environment for a non-sandbox child.

**Relevant code**
- [`env.py#L291-L295`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/env.py#L291-L295) — serializes submitted variables.
- [`job_info.py#L115-L129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/job_info.py#L115-L129) — loads the cached snapshot.
- [`client.py#L1008-L1014`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/client/client.py#L1008-L1014) — merges parent variables into children.
- [`types.py#L758-L789`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/16a8b23048/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py#L758-L789) — adds submitter defaults during serialization.

# Proposed Fix

`run task → IRIS_JOB_ENV → get_job_info().env → IrisClient.submit()` is the leak path. Add a per-submission explicit environment mode for non-sandbox children: use only the supplied `EnvironmentSpec.env_vars`, without parent or submitter variables, while preserving setup scripts and placement constraints. Keep inheritance as the default; document the explicit mode and cover the child submission behavior with a regression test. Cluster-wide `task_env` remains governed by the cluster configuration; sandbox isolation is tracked in #9816.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 [PR #9999](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9999) adds an explicit child environment mode and disables Kubernetes service-link injection for SANDBOX pods. The focused environment and pod tests pass (169 cases). The full Iris suite passed 2,873 cases and failed two outside the changed paths; the controller-identity failure also reproduces on `main`.

**Remaining sandbox plan**
1. Split setup/launcher environment from the model-controlled command environment in the Docker worker and Kubernetes task launchers. Remove runtime `IRIS_*` entries before the command starts while preserving any `IRIS_*` variable explicitly supplied by the job.
2. Pass workdir and venv paths needed by the launcher without exporting them to the command, then test the command's observed environment and task setup, status, logs, and exec on both backends.
3. Keep #9997 open until that contract is verified. #9816 tracks the broader sandbox isolation work.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
tl;dr

PivotRL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21383) is a flavor of RL that was used extensively in Nemotron-Ultra post-training. It operates on existing SFT trajectories to combine the compute efficiency of SFT with the OOD accuracy of E2E RL. PivotRL first executes local, on-policy rollouts and filters for pivots: informative intermediate turns where sampled actions exhibit high variance in outcomes; then it utilizes rewards for functional-equivalent actions rather than demanding strict string matching with the SFT data demonstration.

MarinSkyRL training data resolves to two kinds, a plain directory (`ArtifactDataSource`) and a TaskTrove parquet cohort (`TaskTroveDataSource`). Neither carries per-step annotations.

Scope: a Marin data source that resolves per-step pivot annotations with artifact identity, request plumbing for them, and a `MARIN_SKYRL` pin bump (`lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py:73`) to a MarinSkyRL revision that consumes the annotations and applies step weights in the training loop.

Open questions:

- Compute pivot scores (teacher-forced NLL under the student) as a Marin
  artifact step, or accept only precomputed annotations?
- Carry detection parameters (spike threshold, pivot weight) as named
  `SkyRLSpec` fields or leave them to `config_yaml` and `overrides`?

Done when:

- A pivot-annotated source resolves to a `ResolvedDataSource` whose
  identity covers the annotations, so the step fingerprint changes when
  annotations change.
- `SkyRLLaunchRequest` carries the annotations, and the pinned MarinSkyRL
  commit applies non-uniform step weights end to end.
- Annotation-free specs keep today's fingerprints and training behavior.
- `tests/rl/test_skyrl.py` covers the new source kind and request fields.
- We can reproduce this result from the paper E2E in MarinSkyRL -> 'On GSM8K (200 problems, 182 Kimi K2.5 competition-math traces, Gemma 4 E4B student), pivot-weighted SFT at 2.5x loss scored 80.0% vs 74.5% for uniform SFT against an 85.5% base."

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
Two released NVIDIA datasets are good candidate targets for the first Snowball PivotRL experiment:

- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-SWE-Pivot-v1), pinned at `4947a3c8ea803413a65f9eca14a96ef521b2ddf5`. The current release has 50,308 pivot rows with `trajectory_id`, prefix position, `expected_action`, and profiling counts/pass rate (`pass_rate_total` is 8 in the inspected rows).
- [`nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-RL-Agentic-Terminal-Pivot-v1), pinned at `eaef26944643644c8a3dbbf361ce6128142f5976`. It has 31,111 pivot rows with `expected_answer`, `source_trajectory_uid`, and `pivot_agent_turn_index` from GLM-5.1/Terminus-2 trajectories.

These releases correct the assumption in the issue that no training data is public. They are sufficient for a method-level reproduction, but not an exact reproduction of the paper: the SWE release is not the paper's reported 87,718-example filtered set, and the Terminal release uses a later teacher/task mixture.

Prepare separate SWE and Terminal artifacts first. Split SWE by `trajectory_id` and Terminal by `metadata.source_trajectory_uid`, not by row, so neighboring prefixes from one trajectory cannot cross train/validation. The adapter should map `responses_create_params.input` to `prompt`, preserve tools and request options, carry the expected action/answer and source identity in `extra_info`, and emit a single-turn local functional-verifier environment. SWE can reuse the existing `nemotron_ultra` action comparator after normalizing the released agent name; Terminal needs an `expected_answer` verifier case. The raw Hugging Face rows are not yet SkyRL-shaped and should not be passed directly to `PromptDataset`.

For iteration, use the two Harbor evals already implemented in Marin:

- SWE-bench Verified random-100: `swebench`
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: `tb2`

Both are in-distribution for this experiment and are safe to inspect and hill climb. Keep the policy's OOD suite untouched until the checkpoint and hyperparameters are frozen. The current launcher command is:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model <registered-snowball-pivot-checkpoint> \
  --evals swebench,tb2 \
  --priority interactive \
  --no-wait
```

The checked-in Harbor policies use Terminus-2 + Daytona; `swebench` points at the fixed random-100 set and `tb2` points at Marin's Terminal-Bench 2 dataset. This also gives us a direct comparison with the Snowball R2E-Gym result in #9225.

Proposed training overlay below. Apply it to `cloud/iris/configs/snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml` so the tested Megatron/vLLM placement and model geometry remain unchanged. `<...>` values are immutable prepared artifacts produced from one of the pinned releases above. Run SWE and Terminal as separate primary arms; a balanced mixture is a follow-up experiment.

```yaml
# snowball_pivotrl_split64.yaml: overlay on snowball_ultra_rlvr1_split64.yaml
entrypoint: standard

context_budget:
  request_window_tokens: 65536
  max_turns: 1
  max_new_tokens_per_turn: null  # proposed: use all context remaining after this row's prefix

trainer:
  strategy: megatron
  seed: 42
  algorithm:
    advantage_estimator: grpo
    grpo_norm_by_std: true
    advantage_batch_normalize: false
    eps_clip_low: 0.2
    eps_clip_high: 0.2
    use_entropy_loss: false
    use_kl_in_reward: false
    use_kl_loss: true
    kl_loss_coef: 0.001
    loss_reduction: token_mean
    dynamic_sampling:
      type: null                 # frozen released pivots: closest paper-like arm
      max_sample_batches: 30
      min_replace_ratio: 0.3
      informative_on: unshaped
      min_reward_std: 0.0
  epochs: 1
  max_steps: 130                # paper's disclosed SWE run length
  update_epochs_per_batch: 1
  train_batch_size: 64          # 64 unique pivot prefixes
  policy_mini_batch_size: 1024  # 64 prefixes x 16 responses
  eval_batch_size: 100
  micro_forward_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu: 1
  use_sample_packing: true
  eval_before_train: true
  eval_interval: 10
  ckpt_interval: 10
  max_ckpts_to_keep: 3
  resume_mode: none
  logger: wandb
  project_name: snowball-pivotrl
  # Keep policy/ref Megatron configs and split64 placement unchanged.

generator:
  backend: vllm
  n_samples_per_prompt: 16
  eval_n_samples_per_prompt: 1
  sampling_params:
    temperature: 1.0
    top_p: 1.0
    top_k: -1
  # Keep the tested split64 engine topology and Hermes tool parser unchanged.

data:
  kind: parquet
  train_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/train.parquet>
  val_data:
    - <s3://immutable-artifact/nemotron-{swe|terminal}-pivot/<hf-revision>/validation.parquet>
  shuffle: true
```

The prepared rows should use `env_class: nemotron_ultra`; retain the existing `environment.skyrl_gym.nemotron_ultra` block. Each pivot rollout must terminate after one sampled action and use the local functional verifier.

`max_new_tokens_per_turn: null` is proposed syntax, not accepted by the current launcher. For a single-turn pivot there should be no separate generation budget: set each request's `max_tokens` to `request_window_tokens - tokenized_prefix_length` and let the model use the remaining context. `ContextBudget` currently requires a positive fixed output allowance and subtracts it from every row's prompt allowance; #9176 should make that field nullable for `max_turns: 1` (or add an equivalent remaining-context mode). Reusing the end-to-end RLVR config's 6,528-token cap would truncate valid pivot actions for no methodological reason.

The `64 x 16` geometry yields 1,024 rollout trajectories per trainer step. Confirm that count in the first rollout manifest before a full run. Start with a bounded startup/memory smoke, then run the static arm above. A Marin-specific follow-up can set `dynamic_sampling.type: filter` with `informative_on: unshaped` to replace stale all-pass/all-fail groups online; that is useful, but it is no longer the paper's frozen-pivot method.

The paper does not disclose the KL coefficient. Pre-register `0`, `0.001`, and `0.01` and report all three instead of selecting one retrospectively from SWE-bench/TB2.1. Keep reward shaping disabled so group informativeness is computed from the binary functional outcome.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
The pinned `reasoning-gym==0.1.25` ARC scorers return 0.05 for a correct answer after its metadata passes through JSON. `parse_board` produces tuple grids, but JSON restores `metadata['output']` as list grids. Both `arc_agi` and `rearc` compare these directly.

Reproduce with the installed reasoning-gym package:

```python
import json
from reasoning_gym.arc.rearc import ReArcConfig, ReArcDataset
from reasoning_gym.arc.board_format import format_board

dataset = ReArcDataset(ReArcConfig(size=1, seed=0))
entry = {'metadata': {'output': ((1, 2), (3, 4))}}
answer = format_board(entry['metadata']['output'], dataset.board_format_opts)
print(dataset.score_answer(answer, entry))  # 1.0
print(dataset.score_answer(answer, json.loads(json.dumps(entry))))  # 0.05
```

Expected: JSON transport preserves the reward for the same correct grid. Fix the Verifyit reasoning-gym boundary or its upstream dependency, then verify both ARC variants against correct and incorrect answers before admitting them.

This affects 282 staged TaskTrove rows (149 `arc_agi`, 133 `rearc`). The frozen converter rejects these because its gold-answer check fails. #9970 retains those exclusions; accepting them requires a separate scorer repair. The minimal reproduction above runs without generating an ARC task or starting a container.

Marin receives JSON containing the validated policy, dataset and benchmark metadata, required verifier variables, error categories, and Harbor commit.

The stock `harbor run --config` CLI can execute a job, but it has no machine-readable preflight command that returns those values before Iris submission. Marin's `trial_driver.py` is the small CLI at that boundary: it uses Harbor's API inside the isolated environment for preflight and execution. We could add a preflight JSON command to Harbor and call that directly, but changing the run invocation alone would leave the preflight driver in place.

A subprocess environment cannot satisfy those imports. Eliminating the separate package throughout that stack would mean moving those Harbor-specific imports behind an adapter/CLI boundary, which is a broader refactor. spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Trinity Mini NUPA provides a child-task-level reproduction and rules out partial aggregation.

The Iris child `/benfeuer/eval-20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-a679/eval-nupa-cb8a6a13/0` has three attempts:

- Attempt 0 completed on 2026-10-02 at 06:24:54 UTC, then Iris recorded `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted` and scheduled a retry.
- Attempt 1 wrote and sealed a complete 5,000-item `NUPA5K-Loose` archive. The archive had 4,510 scored responses, 490 classified infrastructure failures, and 2,414 correct answers, so the recovered score was 2,414 / 5,000 = `0.4828`. The tracker sealed that complete attempt on 2026-10-03.
- Iris again recorded the attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` and started attempt 2 at 2026-10-03 10:41:20 UTC. Attempt 2 completed successfully on 2026-10-04 at 15:46:05 UTC and wrote `0.4788` to the same result URI.

Both reported scores cover the full 5,000-item panel. The difference is between complete replays of one stochastic evaluation under one run ID, not between a partial and final aggregate.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

`build_evaluation_batch()` serializes one `run_id` and results path per evaluation. An Iris replay enters the same runner with that identity; the evaluator can reopen the sealed archive, and `write_record()` overwrites the canonical record. The September 27 and October 6 incidents document successful records replaced by retry or cancellation failures.

**Relevant code**
- [`launch.py#L213-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L213-L220) — serializes the run ID and results path
- [`runner.py#L243-L269`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L243-L269) — reuses the path and writes a record
- [`records.py#L319-L325`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L319-L325) — replaces `record.json`
- [`store.py#L175-L181`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L175-L181) — reopening clears the seal

# Attempt isolation and first-success publication

[PR #9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) already changes evaluation scheduling and uses `StepSpec` status to skip successful steps on restart. Its own description identifies the remaining crash window between writing a record and marking the step successful. This plan belongs in that PR or its successor; a separate runner PR would overlap it.

## Design

Keep the launch `run_id` as the stable tracker identity. Allocate a fresh attempt ID when an evaluation actually starts, and write Evalchemy or Harbor output, its FineStore archive, and an attempt record under `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/attempts/{attempt_id}/`. Pass that attempt's results path to the executor, so a retry cannot reopen an earlier sealed archive. Preserve the attempt ID and Iris job IDs in the attempt record for audit.

Publish `{records_prefix}/{run_id}/record.json` only after an attempt's output is sealed and its metrics are validated. Use a storage-conditional update (GCS generation or S3 ETag/create precondition) so the first successful record wins even if a lock expires or two writers race. Failure records may replace an earlier failure while no success exists; after success, later attempts cannot replace the canonical record or its referenced results. A replay that finds a canonical success should return that record path before starting serving or evaluation, including when a previous worker died after publication but before `StepSpec` wrote `SUCCESS`.

Update the launcher, runner, record writer, reporting path, and EvalDash reader together. Existing run pages keep the stable `run_id`; the canonical record points at an immutable attempt's results. Keep old flat-layout records readable for historical runs. A deliberate new evaluation gets a new launch `run_id` instead of changing an existing score.

## Costs and risks

The additional attempt directory and conditional publication path change the persistent layout and require both CoreWeave S3 and GCS semantics to be exercised. Step status and record publication can disagree after a crash; recovery must treat a canonical success as complete. Existing readers that assume results live directly under `{run_id}/results` need updating.

## Testing and completion

Add a regression that publishes a successful, sealed attempt, interrupts before step success, then replays the batch: no new evaluator runs and the canonical record and seal remain byte-for-byte unchanged. Cover failure-then-success, success-then-failure, and two competing publishers; verify that attempt records remain separate and EvalDash keeps the first successful score. Run the repository's local evaluation tests and pre-commit checks, then exercise conditional publication on the configured S3 and GCS backends before landing.

## Open question

Should the canonical path show the latest failed attempt until a success arrives, or should failed attempts appear only in the attempt history? The first option preserves current failed-run visibility; either choice must prevent a failure from replacing success.

comments.body:
🤖 I traced the Evalchemy revision pinned by the September evaluation policies (`c131e5ab`) and the current FineStore write path. The NUPA replay is consistent with the code: the child never restores or checks the prior durable result before starting a new evaluation.

- Evalchemy's `--resume-mode auto` looks for request state under its local `--output_path` ([resume wiring](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/wiring.py#L103-L114)). Marin creates a new `TemporaryDirectory` for that argument on every child invocation; it passes the durable result URI separately as `--finestore_output_path` ([client](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L185-L203), [task loop](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L257-L265)). Thus the retry has no local resume state. The fork opens FineStore only when writing the new aggregate and samples, then seals it ([writer](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/contracts/finestore_output.py#L32-L66)). This is an integration gap, not evidence that Evalchemy tried and failed to restore the completed archive.
- FineStore's writer deliberately clears a seal when it opens an existing archive ([DataStore](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py#L180-L189)). In a local two-writer check, `ReadView.is_sealed()` changed from `True` after the first seal to `False` immediately after the retry opened it. The seal describes the current archive state; it does not make the URI immutable. Marin also submits the Evalchemy child before checking existing results ([runner](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L338-L352)) and writes `record.json` with an unconditional `"w"` open ([record writer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py#L510-L520)).

[#9813](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9813) should skip an evaluation after its StepSpec has recorded success. Its description acknowledges the window between writing a record and marking the step successful. A child retry after sealing, or a replay in that window, can still touch the shared FineStore URI. The child needs a durable, task-specific completion check before running, with configuration and coverage validation, or a separate output URI per attempt plus protected publication of the first success. The archive seal alone is insufficient as a whole-evaluation indicator because Evalchemy seals during each task's output write, before Marin's later validation and normalization.

This conclusion is from the pinned source and a local FineStore check; I did not replay the cited S3 archive. The attempt timelines and score changes in this issue supply the production evidence.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Yes, Evalchemy can resume a partial run when it is restarted with the **same persistent `--output_path`** and a matching fingerprint. Its resume manager records each completed request or pass@k batch with enough payload to reconstruct the result, skips those units on restart, and rejects material fingerprint changes ([manager](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/manager.py#L85-L141), [restore and record](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/manager.py#L199-L243)). Marin currently gives each invocation a fresh temporary `--output_path`, so that recovery state does not survive an Iris retry ([client](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L257-L265)). Evalchemy writes native results and normalized samples to FineStore only after the evaluation completes ([FineStore output](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/contracts/finestore_output.py#L32-L66)); the current archive therefore cannot recover work lost partway through a child run.

A FineStore-backed resume store is feasible without changing the evaluator's unit-level skip/restore logic. I would make that logic persist its fingerprint and completed-unit payloads under the durable task URI using synchronous FineStore transactions, then load them through a read-only `ReadView` on retry. Commit units in bounded batches: a crash would redo at most the uncommitted batch. The normalized `samples` table is not a substitute for these payloads, which also carry the exact generation output and sample identity used to reconstruct scoring ([resume payload use](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/task.py#L390-L435)). FineStore's cache and file-set adapters are best-effort; its transactional API is the appropriate durability boundary ([FineStore docs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/README.md#L12-L43), [cache caveat](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/87579ac1cf39dd805ca664e40177c332b3021e16/lib/finestore/README.md#L122-L129)).

Recovery and final-result protection need separate checks. Read and validate a task-specific completion marker **before** opening the archive for writing, because `DataStore.open` clears an existing seal. A matching completed task should return its existing result without running Evalchemy; an incomplete task should restore committed units and continue. The completion check should include expected coverage and the dataset/task/grader revision; the [current fingerprint](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/blob/c131e5ab84d3014490549ec06d45deb13b5673c2/eval/resume/wiring.py#L25-L35) explicitly omits controlling-file digests. Finally, protect the run-level success record from later attempts. A FineStore seal alone cannot serve as that marker: Evalchemy seals after each task's output write, before Marin finishes its validation and record publication.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Follow-up to #9920 (single-expert transfer: plain SFT, RS-SFT and OPD each moved the CruxEval expert E's gain back into the Snowball student B). Design note is kept by the owner; this issue is the summary and coordination record.

**TL;DR.** Build a second expert E_2 from B the same way as E, in a different domain (MMLU-Pro), then compare four ways of putting both experts' gains into B at once: multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD from E + E_2), SFT on mixed demos, SFT on rejection-sampled mixed demos, and weight merging of B + E + E_2. Every arm is scored on both domains, so the design also measures forgetting (the domain an arm was not trained for) and collapse (GSM8K, GPQA-D, MATH500). Status: data for E_2 prepared and verified; E_2 training awaits approval; no arm has run.

**Questions.**
1. Do the experts themselves collapse in the other domain after GLM SFT? (E on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-D; E_2 on CruxEval; both on GSM8K.)
2. When both experts are transferred into B at once, how much of each domain is recovered and how much of the other is lost?
3. How do MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and merging compare on that, and at what cost?

**Models.** B = `open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5` (unchanged). E = the #9920 CruxEval expert (`…/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`; CruxEval 79.4 / 71.4 vs B 55.4 / 57.8; GPQA-D 44.8% vs B 41.9%, 198 questions × 3 repeats, no observed drop). E_2 = B + full SFT on GLM 5.3 MMLU-Pro traces with E's exact recipe: AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3% warmup then cosine, 3 epochs, fresh optimizer state, frozen router bias, 32 H100.

**E_2 domain and data.** MMLU-Pro (B 44.1%, GLM 5.3 85.8% under the frozen evaluator). The GLM trace collection had indexed the dataset by question text; 200 questions appear in 2–3 prompt variants, so 190 docs carried a wrong gold letter and 175 GLM grades flipped. Every captured doc was re-joined to the pinned dataset (TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro test @ `b189ec765aa7ed75c8acfea42df31fdae71f97be`) by exact question + ordered options and relabelled; B's stored per-doc labels were independently correct (5,303/12,032 = 44.07% under both label sets). Training subset: a seeded, category-proportional draw of whole question groups (every prompt variant of a picked question travels with it): 1,589 questions = 1,606 docs, 1,359 with a usable GLM trace (correct, finished, reasoning present, fits 32,768 tokens under B's template); 729,901 supervised tokens per epoch. Docs without a usable trace stay in the subset denominator untrained. The other 10,426 docs are held out from this fine-tuning and scored as a probe. B on the subset 43.9%, on the remainder 44.1%; GLM 85.7% / 85.9%. Artifacts (SHA-pinned, independently verified): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/`.

**E_2 gate (operational).** Paired gain over B on the subset ≥ 10 pp as a point estimate and lower 95% group-bootstrap bound ≥ 5 pp on the first pass; if the first pass lands in [8, 10) on the gain or [3, 5) on the bound, one second pass is run and the gate is re-evaluated on both passes pooled (never the better pass). GSM8K paired drop over 2 pp stops the arm. CruxEval, GPQA-D, MATH500 and the held-out score are reported, not gated.

**Frozen evaluator.** As #9920: Evalchemy `c131e5ab`, vLLM H100x8 DP8+EP8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap (28,672 for GPQA-D), thinking on, temperature 1.0 unseeded. MMLU-Pro runs always score all 12,032 docs; subset and held-out numbers are sliced from the record against the canonical labels, with bootstrap intervals that resample question groups.

**Arms (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the same 3,206 prompts = 1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro; one checkpoint per epoch).**
- MOPD from E + E_2: 4 rollouts per prompt, CruxEval prompts scored by E and MMLU-Pro prompts by E_2 (MarinSkyRL routed teachers), one teacher node each.
- Mixed SFT: one demo per prompt (E's sample 0 from the #9920 k=8 CruxEval pool; E_2's sample 0 from a new k=8 collection on the 1,606), the SFT counterpart of MOPD on the same prompts and epochs (prompt-matched, not token-matched).
- Mixed SFT-RS: first execution-correct (CruxEval) or answer-correct (MMLU-Pro) sample per prompt from the two k=8 pools; uncovered prompts stay in the denominators. Uses verifier access the other arms do not have.
- Merge B + E + E_2: #9974 tools with B as anchor and E, E_2 as donors, task arithmetic B + a·(E−B) + b·(E_2−B) over a small coefficient grid plus TIES and DARE-TIES; CPU only, no training.
- Dropped: OPD from E_2 alone and plain SFT from E_2 demos alone (the single-expert question was answered in #9920).

**Selection and reporting.** As #9920: prefer the final checkpoint when it is similar or better on every target metric (similar = paired 95% CI includes 0, an operational threshold); otherwise a second pass on the last two checkpoints and the two-pass means decide. Costs in H100-hours from Iris task durations (method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298); full-run figures labelled as such; demo generation counted once; failed-eval overhead separate. One consolidated final comment; no running log here.

**Budget (planning estimates).** E_2 ≈ 30–40 H100-h; k=8 E_2 demos on 1,606 prompts ≈ 2; MOPD ≈ 300–500 (7 nodes; set by the smoke run); mixed SFT and SFT-RS ≈ 60–120 each; merge CPU only; evaluations ≈ 150.

**Decision log.**
- 2026-10-09: MMLU-Pro chosen as E_2's domain (GPQA-D too small to train on: 198 questions). Subset = whole question groups, ~1,600 docs; remainder held out as a probe. GLM labels repaired and verified by two agents; B labels confirmed. Arms fixed to MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS, merge(B,E,E_2); OPD-from-E_2 and E_2-only SFT dropped. New issue opened rather than continuing in #9920.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
Try **per-head MuonH** on the MLA kv-latent up-projections: orthogonalize each head's `(kv_lora, head_dim)` block independently instead of the full `(kv_lora, n·head_dim)` matrix. Per `experiments/grug/moe/ablation_runbook.md`.

**Branch:** https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grug/moe-abl/per-head-muon-kv

## Verbatim prompt

> lets follow ablation doc and make a new issue. lets try per head muon, where the projections from kv_latent -> k and v have muon applied seperately per head. this way, the projection from 512->1024 is replaced with 512->128. lets also run at d2048, where we replace 512->2048 with 512->128. only apply the change to the K and V projections. Leave Q as is. Apply in whichever way is simplest: custom reshape in optimizer, or storing parameters in stacked shape. This should be 2 runs, one for each size.

## Change under test

`w_uk` (kv_latent → k_nope) and `w_uv` (kv_latent → v) are `(kv_lora=512, n·head_dim)`. Muon currently Newton-Schulzes them as one matrix. This ablation orthogonalizes **each head's `(512, 128)` block separately** — so the `512→n·128` projection becomes `n` independent `512→128` orthogonalizations:
- **d1024**: n=8 → `512→1024` becomes 8× `512→128`.
- **d2048**: n=16 → `512→2048` becomes 16× `512→128`.

**Only K and V** (`w_uk`, `w_uv`). **Q (`w_uq`) is unchanged** (full-matrix Muon).

Implementation (simplest = **custom reshape in the optimizer**): `SCALE_MUON_PER_HEAD_KV=1` makes `grugmuon`'s `transform_array` split the trailing `n·128` axis of `w_uk`/`w_uv`, vmap the replicated NS over the (head, scan-layer) batch, and reshape back. No model/forward/sharding change, so scan stays on and the runs are directly comparable to the `mla-base` LR-sweep points. Verified: each head block is semi-orthogonal (col err ≈ 0.078, normal for 5-step quintic) and differs from full-matrix NS.

## Runs (2, MLA, ablation defaults, scan on)

Both: MLA `SCALE_MLA_HEAD_MULT=1`, qk 192, all-global (`SCALE_SLIDING_WINDOW=4096`), datakit 2-phase, evals on, s3, MuonH base LR, `SCALE_MUON_PER_HEAD_KV=1`.

spillover_issues.author: weaverbot
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

The opencode RL "literal log" — how a CLI agent's per-token training signal (`token_ids`/`logprobs`/`chat_history`) is recovered for TIS — is today a single append-only JSONL file (10s of MB) written by the harbor RecordProxy and read by MarinSkyRL's `TerminalBenchGenerator`. Both sides hand-roll the framing independently:

- **writer** (harbor/otagent): appends newline-delimited JSON to one shared, growing, worker-local file.
- **reader** (MarinSkyRL): incremental byte-offset reads, partial-line carry, inode/shrink rotation detection, and a hand-built `{trial_id: [entries]}` index (see `LiteralLogStore` in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#49).

This is fragile (no corruption detection, partial records, rotation edge cases) and is an anti-pattern on object storage: a single mutable file appended-while-read maps badly onto GCS/S3 — no efficient append, no tailing an open object, eventual consistency.

Replace the ad-hoc JSONL-file contract with **one consolidated reader/writer interface** — a shared library used by BOTH sides — that owns the record schema, framing, coordination, and per-trial indexing, and is object-storage-native. Cross-repo cleanup: the writer lives in harbor/otagent (here), the reader in MarinSkyRL, so the shared interface belongs in this repo and both depend on it.

### Definition of Done

- A shared LogStore module (writer + reader) with a single defined record schema + framing, replacing the JSONL-file contract — neither side hand-rolls parsing or indexing.
- **Object-storage-native layout**: immutable *sealed segments + a manifest* (list-a-prefix, read-sealed-objects), not one mutable growing file. Works on local FS **and** `gs://` without the append-while-read hazard. This rules out SQLite/WAL (needs local POSIX locking) and single-file Parquet (can't tail a half-written file) — see the format analysis in marin-community/MarinSkyRL#49.
- Smarter than 10s-of-MB of JSON: at minimum length-framed + CRC'd records (corruption detection); columnar/compressed sealed segments (Arrow IPC or Parquet-per-segment) where scan efficiency is wanted.
- Per-trial lookup + write/read coordination are library features, tested once.
- harbor RecordProxy writes via it; MarinSkyRL's `LiteralLogStore` is replaced by (or thinly wraps) the shared reader, with a **dual-read compatibility window** (reader accepts old JSONL + new segments during rollout, since the two sides ship in separately-built images).

Refs: marin-community/MarinSkyRL#49 (`LiteralLogStore` + format-migration analysis), marin-community/MarinSkyRL#51 (e2e gate that would exercise it), marin-community/MarinSkyRL#37 / #38 / #41.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + confirm actionability
- [x] Locate the writer (harbor RecordProxy) and reader (MarinSkyRL `LiteralLogStore`) in this repo
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues)
- [x] Post research + proposed approach

# Research

The design goal (object-storage-native manifest + sealed-segment LogStore replacing the append-while-read JSONL contract) is well-specified with a concrete DoD, so it's actionable — but it's a **large, cross-repo design change**, not a self-contained bug fix, so this is an analysis comment for human review, not a PR.

Blocking scope finding: **neither endpoint the issue names exists in `marin-community/marin`.** No `RecordProxy`, `LiteralLogStore`, `otagent`, `opencode`, or literal-log JSONL code is present. The writer lives in harbor/OT-Agent and the reader in `MarinSkyRL` (`#49`) — both separate repos. What *is* here:

- `harbor_evaluator.py` — only a CLI wrapper around `harbor run` that parses trial JSON; it does not read/write the literal log.
- PR #7246 (`feuer/agentic-evals-extraction`) extracts agentic-evals infra *out of* OT-Agent into `experiments/agentic_evals/` (presets/serve/harness/runtime/results/backends) — and pointedly does **not** include the RecordProxy / literal-log writer.

So before any implementation: **where does the shared library live, given the writer and reader are built into separately-shipped images in two other repos?** That ownership decision is a prerequisite and belongs to a human.

**Relevant code / prior art**
- [`rollout_storage.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_storage.py) — already the exact pattern the issue asks for: a `create_reader()/create_writer()` config interface with `FileRolloutReader`/`FileRolloutWriter` writing **one immutable file per batch over fsspec** (glob-a-prefix, read-sealed-files, no append-while-read). Object-storage-native; works on local FS and `gs://`.
- [`harbor_evaluator.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/harbor_evaluator.py) — the only harbor surface in-repo (CLI wrapper, not the log path).
- PR #7246 — OT-Agent extraction; the natural in-repo home for a writer, but currently excludes it.

# Proposed approach

Follow the `rollout_storage.py` model rather than inventing a new format layer — it already solves the append-while-read hazard the issue calls out.

- **Layout**: writer emits immutable sealed segments under a per-run prefix (`<prefix>/<worker>/<seq>.arrow`) plus a `manifest.json`; reader lists the prefix and reads sealed objects. No mutable growing file, so GCS eventual consistency and lack of append/tailing are non-issues.
- **Records**: length-framed + CRC32C per record for corruption detection; segment payload as Arrow IPC (columnar, compressed, scan-efficient) — rules out SQLite/WAL (POSIX locking) and single-file Parquet (can't tail a half-written file), matching the `#49` analysis.
- **Per-trial index**: `{trial_id: [(segment, row_range)]}` built from the manifest, a library feature tested once — deletes the reader's hand-rolled byte-offset/inode/shrink-rotation logic.
- **Dual-read window**: reader accepts legacy JSONL *and* new segments during rollout (the two sides ship in separate images).
- **Home**: put the shared lib where both sides can depend on it. Given the writer's in-repo landing spot is #7246's `experiments/agentic_evals/`, and the closest reusable code is `lib/marin/.../rl/rollout_storage.py`, a small `logstore` module under `lib/` that #7246 and MarinSkyRL both import is the least-duplicating option — but this needs sign-off since it creates a new cross-repo dependency.

Recommend a human confirm the ownership/home question and whether to generalize `rollout_storage.py` vs. add a sibling `logstore` before implementation starts.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
_Filed by an AI agent on behalf of **@penfever** (LAION / OpenThoughts), labeled `agent-generated` per the repo's [AI-generated contributions](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/dev-guide/contributing.md) policy._

@rjpower — do you think we could surface some summary stats from **Iris finelog** that would let us track Marin **preemptible compute use weekly**, drop it into **MWS** as a summary section, and map it to **users** (certainly) and ideally to **public GitHub issues**? I think it would give everyone greater confidence about "where the compute is all going."

The motivation is transparency. "Where did the compute go this week?" currently gets answered anecdotally. A weekly, per-user (and ideally per-issue) rollup of preemptible TPU-hours — plus how much we lose to preemption churn — would give the team one shared, citable picture instead.

### Why this looks tractable today

Iris already carries most of the raw material:

- **Attribution is first-class.** Jobs carry `owner_principal` / `submitting_user` (controller.proto), and there's a `ListUsers` API — so per-user rollups don't need to parse names out of job paths.
- **Per-job compute + waste is already derivable from finelog job history.** `scripts/iris/analyze_job_history.py` paginates the full history and reports `total_runtime_s`, `iris_preemption_count`, per-cycle placement/serve, etc. Aggregate that across a week by user × cluster × accelerator and you get chip-hours plus a preemption-overhead figure.
- **Region / accelerator are on the placement**, so we can split v5p vs v6e and us-central1 vs us-east5 vs europe-west4.

### Proposed shape

1. A weekly job that reads finelog (or reuses the `analyze_job_history` aggregation) and emits, per ISO week:
   - preemptible TPU **chip-hours** by **user**, by **cluster/region**, by **accelerator type**;
   - a **preemption-overhead** metric — chip-hours (or wall-time) lost to preempt → re-place churn vs. productive compute. This is the "what are we actually paying for preemptible" number, and it's the one people are surprised by;
   - top-N jobs by chip-hours.
2. Drop a compact table into **MWS** each week (the same weekly-summary artifact the team already reads), so it shows up where people are already looking.
3. **Stretch — map to GitHub issues.** This is the one piece of glue that doesn't exist cleanly today. Users are easy (`owner_principal`); issues need a job → issue link — e.g. a launch-time convention (`issue=#NNNN` in job labels/metadata) or a maintained lookup. Worth deciding whether that's in scope for v1 or a follow-up.

### Open questions

- **Finelog retention** — is a full ISO-week of job/task events reliably inside the retention window, or do we need to snapshot the weekly aggregate before it ages out? (This probably decides whether the weekly job is "read finelog directly" vs. "roll up incrementally into a durable table.")
- **Preemptible vs. reserved** — preemptible-only, or report both with a split?
- **"Productive vs. wasted" definition** — do cold-compile / resume-scan chip-hours count as overhead, or only the re-placement gaps between attempts?
- **Attribution granularity** — user-level for v1 with issue-level as a fast-follow, or hold for the issue link?

Happy to prototype the finelog → weekly-aggregate step if the shape sounds right — the per-job pieces are already there in `analyze_job_history`; the new parts are the weekly grouping, the overhead metric, and the MWS drop.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Scoped and published as a design PR: #7387 (`design.md` / `research.md` / `spec.md` under `.agents/projects/iris_compute_accounting/`). Ran the codex peer review you asked for, plus a fable and an architect pass — they found two load-bearing things that reshaped the doc.

**On your "iris event `<started/preempted/resumed/finished> <user> <time> <resources>`" intuition** — that's exactly the missing piece and it's the core of the proposal: a durable `iris.accounting` finelog namespace, one row per terminated attempt. The catch the review surfaced is that it **must be captured at terminalization inside the controller**, not read back weekly. Zone/region/preemptible live on the `workers` row, and `remove_worker` deletes that row and NULLs `task_attempts.worker_id` in the *same transaction* that terminalizes a preempted attempt (`writes.py:734`) — so a post-hoc query sees NULL placement for the entire preemption cohort at t=0, and `worker_retention` is only 24h anyway. (`iris.task_event` is a same-named red herring: k8s scheduling verdicts, ~1h retention.) So there's no "just query finelog weekly" shortcut for the preemptible split — the emit is the work.

**On prometheus MFU** — good news: MFU-per-job is *already* durable in the finelog `telltale` namespace (`levanter_throughput_mfu`), and Grafana already reads it. Two caveats: it's Levanter-training-only (vLLM/Zephyr emit nothing), and TPUs have **no** hardware duty-cycle telemetry at all, so for TPUs MFU is the only "are the chips busy" signal. "Downtime" needs the same terminalization capture (recovery-idle = gap between a preempted attempt finishing and the next starting).

**One honesty flag on the headline number:** "chip-hours lost to preemption" as full preempted-attempt runtime is a large over-count — Levanter checkpoints and resumes, and user cancels land as KILLED-with-started rows. The doc reports a labeled *upper bound* plus a separately-computed recovery-idle figure instead.

Genuinely-your-call Open Questions (in `design.md`): the emit's delivery guarantee (best-effort + reconciliation vs. transactional outbox), where the `MARIN_ISSUE` number comes from, and whether to measure attribution coverage (how much compute is `local_admin` vs. a real email) before building. I can start Phase 0 — the cheap attribution-coverage probe — while the design gets eyes.

🤖 Fair hit — the first draft described joins without the queries. I went and ran them against live finelog (DuckDB over the GCS parquet), so these are real numbers, and rewrote the spec query-first. Pushed to #7387.

**How you find MFU for a job.** Levanter already forwards `throughput/mfu` to the durable finelog `telltale` namespace as `levanter_throughput_mfu`, tagged with `job_id` (iris root) and `run` (wandb). Two gotchas the real data exposed that the abstract version got wrong: `process_index` is NULL (so my "dedup to process 0" returned nothing), and on a multislice job every worker forwards the same value — so collapse per step first:

```sql
WITH per_step AS (
  SELECT job_id, run, ts, any_value(value) AS mfu
  FROM "telltale"
  WHERE name='levanter_throughput_mfu' AND ts >= {{from}} AND ts < {{to}}
  GROUP BY job_id, run, ts)
SELECT job_id, run, round(avg(mfu),1) AS mean_mfu, count(*) steps
FROM per_step GROUP BY job_id, run ORDER BY steps DESC;
```

Real output right now:
```
/runner/iris-run-job-20260718-074819   canary-tpu-...          19.1   139
/runner/iris-run-job-20260718-113025   grug-multislice-smoke   4.5      9
```
(`_mean_mfu`, `_p10/50/90_mfu` are forwarded too, so percentiles are free.)

**What other queries.** Two more run today with no new infra — full SQL + real output in [spec.md §1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/issue-7353/.agents/projects/iris_compute_accounting/spec.md):
- Preemptions by pool/zone from `iris.provisioning` — last 7d: v6e-4/us-east1-d **471**, v5p-8/us-east5-a **311**.
- Host-hours by user from `iris.task` (its `task_id` is `/user/job/...`, so `split_part(task_id,'/',2)` is the user) — last 24h: eczech **21.6h**, larry **12.4h**, michaelryan **4.7h**.

So Phase 1 is a real report on existing finelog. The one thing finelog can't give is **chip-hours** (iris.task has no device count) or the **preemptible/region split** (that placement is deleted from the DB the instant a preempted attempt terminates — `remove_worker`, `writes.py:734`, 24h worker retention). That's the only reason for the new `iris.accounting` row in Phase 2.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment validated the FP8 changes from PR #7079 against a bf16 control at the row-13 Grug MoE scale, using identical seed and data order and a full 24,000-step schedule on H100s. After smoke debugging reduced the run to one 8-H100 node per arm and fixed allocator fragmentation with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, both arms completed cleanly. The loss-curve gate passed: FP8 ended with a matched-step gap of about +0.0040, flat through the cooldown tail and inside the <=0.01 acceptance bar, while running about 5.5% faster by throughput. The campaign also found two follow-ups that do not block the gate: BFC allocator fragmentation can silently deadlock training collectives without `cuda_async`, and FP8 currently uses about 1.66x the bf16 transient step arena because XLA keeps cast/transpose FP8 operands resident for backward GEMMs.

### Helpful links
- [Final result comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7298#issuecomment-5010209991)
- [W&B overlay group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/groups/fp8-loss-val-7079)
- [Final comparison artifact](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Part of #6699. Validates PR #7079 (FP8 expert GEMMs + FP8 EP wire + FP8 dense GEMMs for attention/shared-expert) against a bf16 control on real data — the loss-curve gate flagged in the PR before FP8 defaults can flip.

**Motivation:** before FP8 can become a default, we need evidence that enabling it does not perturb the training loss at production scale. This experiment runs a bf16 control (main) and an FP8 test arm (PR #7079) in parallel on the CoreWeave H100s from identical init and data order, saving the full per-step loss trajectory for both, and compares them. The run is sized (~8 h, cached in-cluster dataset, full LR schedule) to show substantial loss movement while resolving 0.01-level precision deltas — using the cluster-resident SlimPajama cache to avoid cross-region data costs and staying within a 64-H100 budget.

## Design

Two arms in parallel on cw-us-east-02a, 4 nodes / 32 H100 each (64 total):

| arm | code | precision |
|---|---|---|
| `fp8val-bf16-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val-ctl` = main + launcher | bf16 |
| `fp8val-fp8-*` | `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val` = PR #7079 merged with main + launcher | `GrugFp8Config(wire=True, dense=True)` |

- **Model:** row-13 flagship shape — d2560, 26 layers, 64 experts top-4 (+shared), MHA 20×128, seq 4096, sliding window 2048, qk_mult 1.3, ~18B params; `ring` MoE backend, EP8 intra-node, FSDP over 4 nodes, `gpu_fa4_cute` attention, `recompute_all` remat. Identical in both arms; seed 0 in both (same init + data order).
- **Optimizer:** production MuonH (`lr=1e-3`, `adam_lr=1e-4`, warmup 10%, cooldown to 0) run through the **full schedule** — #6486 showed precision gaps surface in the cooldown tail, so a truncated schedule can show false parity.
- **Data:** SlimPajama-6B llama3-tokenized cache already materialized under this cluster's `MARIN_PREFIX` (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin`, in-cluster LOTA endpoint) — zero cross-region traffic. Feistel block shuffle.
- **Budget:** ~11k steps × 128 seqs × 4096 tok ≈ 5.8B tokens/arm, sized from measured H100 throughput to finish inside ~8 h (final step count calibrated by a short smoke run). Precedent: #6486 resolved 0.01-level loss deltas at 1.4B tokens.
- **Trajectory:** W&B project `marin_moe`, group `fp8-loss-val-7079`, `log_every=1` (per-step `train/loss`).

**Acceptance:** matched-step train-loss overlay; gap ≤0.01 at end of schedule (the #6486 threshold for a meaningful difference), with specific attention to the last 10% (cooldown tail). Divergence, NaNs, or a growing gap fails the gate.

Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` on `research/mcwitt/7079-fp8-loss-val`.

Note: not filed under the #4281 recipe-ablation family — this is infra/precision validation for #6699, not a recipe-change experiment.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Full A/B launched 2026-07-17 13:32 UTC after nine smoke rounds: `/mwittmann/fp8val-bf16-full1` vs `/mwittmann/fp8val-fp8-full1` on cw-us-east-02a.

**Final configuration** (revised from the issue body's design during smoke debugging — full trail in `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md`):

- 1 node × 8 H100 per arm (16 total), EP8, **batch 16** × seq 4096, **24000 steps ≈ 1.57B tokens/arm** (≥ the 1.44B that resolved 0.01-level deltas in #6486). Model/optimizer/data/seed as designed (row-13 shapes, MuonH full schedule to zero LR, SlimPajama-6B cluster-local cache, seed 0 both arms).
- Tracker: json_logger (per-step `train/loss` in job logs) — no WANDB key was reachable on the submit host; trajectories will be harvested and plotted here.
- No periodic checkpoints (`FP8VAL_CHECKPOINTS=local`).

**Operational findings from the smoke ladder** (each cost a round; logged for reuse):
1. Multi-host XLA sharded-autotuning rendezvous hangs the 4-node compile → `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false`.
2. `experiments/grug/dispatch.py` forwarded only `XLA_FLAGS`, silently dropping `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` → train tasks ran at the 0.75 default pool and OOM'd; forwarding widened to `XLA_*` (+ `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`) on both experiment branches — candidate for upstreaming.
3. Row-13 (26 unrolled layers) does not fit 4-node FSDP (`data=4`) or 2-node EP16 at B64 on 80GB H100s (program peak 89 GiB; matches the June spike's "B64+L26 HBM wall").
4. **FP8 needs ~4 GB more than bf16 at B32** where the pre-merge bench harness fit — possible memory regression from the main merge or a real-trainer×FP8 interaction; open follow-up.
5. **The 10-minute async time-checkpoint deadlocks the run against training collectives** (all bf16 "NCCL clique stalls" and one FP8 step-10 OOM sit exactly at the first save; reproduced on three different nodes). Avoided here by disabling periodic saves; deserves its own issue.
6. bf16 also stalls NCCL comm-init at mem fraction 0.95 but not 0.90; FP8 needs 0.95. Arms run their proven fraction (allocator pool size does not affect numerics).

ETA: fp8 ~6h, bf16 ~6.7h + ~15 min compile. Results (matched-step deltas, final-loss gap vs the ≤0.01 acceptance bar, cooldown-tail zoom) to follow at completion.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Root cause of every training wedge found — and it is neither log reads nor checkpoint saves.**

Full-history post-mortems of all terminal runs (smoke9, full1–full3b) show one identical signature in all five wedges: a **BFC allocator failure to allocate the train step's contiguous scratch chunk** — `bfc_allocator.cc ran out of memory trying to allocate 22.66GiB` (bf16 arms) / `40.68GiB` (fp8 arms) on 1–5 of 8 GPUs — followed ~10 s later by the permanent `Acquire clique` rendezvous stall. Allocator dumps show the pool only ~40% occupied at failure: **fragmentation, not exhaustion**. The device threads whose allocation fails never join the 8-way clique rendezvous, so the remaining ranks wait forever — a silent XLA deadlock instead of a raised OOM.

Both earlier theories are retracted with evidence:
- **Log reads (FP8VAL-003b): refuted.** `iris job logs` is served by the standalone finelog server over on-disk parquet (fed by the logship sidecar); it never enters the task process (the in-task uvicorn is the metrics telltale). Timeline agrees: bf16-full2 *survived* the heavy 400k/600k-line harvests at 18:08 UTC and wedged at 19:09 with no heavy read within 10 min; the blamed 900k harvest ran at 19:19 — after the stall.
- **Checkpoint saves (FP8VAL-003c): demoted to a perturbation.** Single-node saves have no barrier/collective; their alloc/free churn just re-carves the pool (both save-adjacent wedges landed 3–11 s after the commit callback). Checkpoint-less arms died identically after hours of slow fragmentation.

Side finding, now quantified: **fp8's largest step temp is 40.68 GiB vs bf16's 22.66 GiB at the identical B16 config** — the fp8 memory regression to bisect, and why fp8 arms always wedged first (needs 57% of the ~72 GiB pool contiguous).

Mitigation for any resubmit: `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR=cuda_malloc_async` (VMM-backed, immune to BFC fragmentation — the allocator's own hint). full4 (running) predates this finding and has no such flag; recovery commands are pre-staged with it. Details in logbook entry FP8VAL-004.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **fp8 memory regression attributed** (compile-only probe, one 8×H100 node, AOT-compiles the exact row-13 step bf16 vs fp8 without running it).

`compiled.memory_analysis()`:

| arm | temp arena | args/output/alias |
|---|---|---|
| bf16 | 22.65 GiB | 29.88 GiB |
| fp8 | 37.67 GiB | 29.89 GiB |

Persistent state (args/output/alias) is **byte-identical** — fp8 adds nothing to params/grads/opt-state. The whole **+15.0 GiB is transient peak** in the single fused train step.

Per-dtype arena composition (from XLA `buffer-assignment.txt`; Δ = fp8 − bf16):

| dtype | Δ (GiB) | what |
|---|---|---|
| f8e4m3fn | **+5.0** | forward fp8 operands |
| u8 (fp8-as-u8) | **+3.3** | transposed dual-write fp8 operand copies |
| f8e5m2 | **+0.8** | backward fp8 gradient operands |
| f32 | +4.1 | scale / dequant / amax / accumulation scratch |
| bf16 | +4.0 | extra intermediates around quantize ops |

**The bf16 arena contains zero float8 tensors; the fp8 arena adds ~9 GiB of float8-family data.** XLA materializes each large linear's quantized operand *and its transposed layout for the backward GEMM* and keeps them resident across the fused forward+backward, rather than requantizing in each GEMM prologue. The +4 f32 and +4 bf16 are the requantization scaffolding. So this is dual-write/mixed-dtype operand residency — **not** custom_vjp remat-pinning (bf16 grew only ~4 of the 15 GiB).

Highest-leverage reduction: recompute the transposed fp8 operand in the backward instead of stashing it (the e4m3 + u8-transpose pair is ~8.3 GiB). Real fp8-wiring overhead, tracked as a follow-up separate from the loss validation. Probe: `experiments/grug/moe/fp8val_mem_probe.py`; logbook FP8VAL-005.

Separately, the training wedge (FP8VAL-004) is fixed by `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement — note this is the JAX var, not TF's `TF_GPU_ALLOCATOR`). bf16 control now clears the fragmentation cliff; both arms running.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **RESULT: loss-curve gate PASSED.** Both arms completed the full 24,000-step schedule (1.57B tokens/arm) cleanly on the `cuda_async` allocator — `fp8val-fp8-full4` and `fp8val-bf16-full6`, seed 0, identical data order.

**Matched-step train loss (FP8 − bf16), all 23,998 steps:**
- mean **+0.0039**, median +0.0038, σ 0.0028, max single-step |Δ| 0.14 (noise)
- no growth: first 2k +0.0034 → mid +0.0029 → **cooldown tail (last 10%) +0.0040**
- final 200-step mean loss: **bf16 3.084 / FP8 3.088 → +0.0040**

**Verdict: PASS** — final matched-step gap **+0.0040**, well inside the ≤0.01 bar (#6486), flat through the cooldown tail (the region #6486 flagged as where precision gaps surface), no NaNs/Infs. Enabling FP8 (wire+dense+grouped GEMMs) does not perturb the training loss at row-13 scale.

**Throughput:** 70.1k / 73.9k tok/s (**1.055×**), MFU 15.09% / 15.92%. On wall-clock (x rescaled by ∫1/throughput), FP8 reaches any given loss ~4.4% sooner and finished 24k in **6.03h vs 6.31h** (~17 min ahead).

Final artifact (4 panels — loss vs step, loss vs wall-clock, Δ with ±0.01 band, throughput): https://claude.ai/code/artifact/99ec4cac-2537-494c-b9e2-1b285311fa32

**Two infra findings from the campaign (both tracked, neither blocks the gate):**
1. Every training "wedge" was a **BFC fragmentation OOM → silent NCCL clique deadlock** at ~42% pool occupancy — *not* heavy log reads or checkpoint saves (both investigated and exonerated). Fix: `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` (VMM allocator, no contiguity requirement). Worth landing as the default for FP8 grug runs.
2. FP8's transient step arena is **1.66× bf16** (+15 GiB), attributed by a compile-only probe to the **cast-transpose dual-write** (caching the transposed FP8 operand for the backward) — a deliberate TE-style speed optimization, bounded and sharding-friendly, not a blocker. Follow-up for #7079 if a memory-marginal config adopts FP8.

Logbook `.agents/logbooks/7079-fp8-loss-val.md` (FP8VAL-006) sealed with full TL;DR.

spillover_issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
spillover_issues.body:
Child of #6037.

## Description
The pooled fast-transformer quality scorer (#7040) emits a calibrated score in `[0,1]` and buckets it at fixed `0.2` cutpoints; a monotonic calibration anchors those cutpoints to the absolute oracle quality levels (1–5). Decide whether that is the right bucketization for building the training mix, vs quantiles or another scheme.

Requirement: buckets must be **coherent** — a bucket means a consistent quality level, comparable across heterogeneous sources — **and** large enough to be a usable unit to mix and consume in training.

Options and trade-offs:
- **Absolute threshold (current)**: bucket = absolute level, so a source's bucket mix reflects its true quality composition (math piles into q3/q4, safety into q1). But the tails are thin — on the 100B run q0 = 1.9%, q4 = 4.6% — so the extreme buckets may be too small to be usable mix units.
- **Quantiles**: each bucket is large by construction (equal mass), but relative-to-distribution. Per-source flattens every source to 20/20/20/20/20 and erases the quality signal; global drifts with corpus composition and drops the absolute-level anchor (loses cross-corpus comparability).
- **Other**: absolute cutpoints with merged/floored thin tails; a hybrid (absolute cutpoints plus a min-bucket-size floor); or fewer / asymmetric bands sized for the mix.

Bucketization lives in `experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/score.py` (calibration remap + `np.digitize` on `BUCKET_EDGES`); calibration is fit in `calibrate.py`.

### Definition of Done
- Bucketization scheme chosen and documented with rationale, satisfying both properties: coherent / cross-source-comparable buckets **and** each bucket large enough to serve as a mix unit.
- Applied in `score.py` / `calibrate.py` and reflected in the July-hero mix construction.
